books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

primary_sources: Photograph of the crowd outside the New York Stock Exchange, October 29, 1929

stimulus.text: A photograph taken on October 29, 1929, shows a large crowd gathered on Wall Street outside the New York Stock Exchange on the day of the stock market crash. Men in suits and hats fill the street between tall buildings, with automobiles stopped among them.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph taken October 29, 1929. Public domain (pre-1930); via Wikimedia Commons.

source: original; stimulus photograph October 29, 1929, public domain
stem: President Hoover's claim in October 1929 that the economy rested “on a sound and prosperous basis” is best understood as

options.text: a warning that the stock market would soon collapse
options.misconception: A warning would say trouble was coming. Hoover said the opposite: the economy was sound.

options.text: an admission that banks were already failing
options.misconception: Hoover admitted no such thing in October 1929. He said the economy was sound, not that banks were failing.

options.text: a promise of direct federal relief for the unemployed
options.misconception: Hoover refused direct federal relief throughout his presidency. The statement promises nothing of the kind.

options.text: a reassurance that underestimated the crash's spread

rationales.A: Background from the books: Hoover said the economy rested on a sound and prosperous basis, a reassurance, not a warning.
rationales.B: Background from the books: bank failures did surge after the crash, but Hoover's October 1929 words denied trouble, they did not admit it.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Hoover feared direct federal payments would foster dependence, and he refused them even as the Depression deepened.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Hoover saw the heart of the economy as the production of goods, not the stock market, so he judged the crash a Wall Street matter. The credit collapse then spread to banks, factories, and jobs.
rationales.general:
1. Read Hoover's words: the economy was sound and prosperous.
2. Ask what he was doing: calming the public after the crash.
3. Ask what he missed. Background from the books: the crash froze credit, banks failed, and factories closed.
4. His reassurance underestimated how far the crash would spread.
Remember: a president's calm words are evidence of confidence, so check them against what happened next.
